summary: A copy of a proposal for a Memorandum of Understanding based Protocol Supporting Organization, submitted to ICANN on April 23, 1999. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A written offer to ICANN on how protocol groups could help guide it.

subtitle: A proposal for how protocol standards organizations should advise ICANN

tldr.problem: ICANN needs a way for Internet protocol standards organizations to provide input on protocol parameter assignments, and needs clear criteria for which organizations can participate.
tldr.mechanism: This proposal describes a Protocol Support Organization (PSO) with a Protocol Council of representatives from standards development organizations, plus annual open meetings and transparent procedures.
tldr.outcome: This proposal was submitted to ICANN in April 1999 and led directly to the signed Memorandum of Understanding (RFC 2691) that created the actual PSO.

today: RFC 2690 is Informational and remains unobsoleted. It documents the proposal that directly led to RFC 2691, the signed Memorandum of Understanding that created the Protocol Support Organization in July 1999. The PSO operated until 2004.

sections.title: What the PSO Is and Why It Matters
sections.content:
This document is a copy of a proposal submitted to ICANN (the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) on April 23, 1999. It proposes creating a Protocol Support Organization (PSO), an advisory body within ICANN's framework that brings together standards development organizations (SDOs) to advise on protocol matters.

The proposal explains that protocol parameter assignments (such as protocol numbers, port numbers, and other registry resources) should be managed by the organizations that developed the protocols, not by a centralized body. The PSO would coordinate between these organizations and ICANN.
sections.eli5: Internet protocol standards groups wanted a formal way to tell ICANN which organizations should get to hand out protocol numbers and similar resources.

sections.title: Structure of the Proposed PSO
sections.content:
The proposal describes three main parts. First, a Protocol Council of up to 12 members selected by SDO signatories (each SDO nominates council members by its own procedures). Council members serve two-year terms. Second, an annual General Assembly open to all interested individuals, held in conjunction with major SDO meetings. Third, a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) that binds ICANN and the participating SDOs to shared governance principles.

The Protocol Council would nominate 3 Directors to the ICANN Board and advise the board on matters related to protocol parameter assignment. The council would also help SDOs resolve conflicts over protocol parameter policies.
sections.eli5: The PSO would have a small group (the Council) that makes decisions, plus yearly public meetings where anyone can talk, and a signed agreement that says how everyone will work together.

sections.title: Criteria for Eligible Standards Organizations
sections.content:
The proposal establishes objective criteria that a standards development organization must meet to join the PSO. An SDO must be open, international, and voluntary. It must demonstrate active membership of more than 1,000 individuals (or 100 companies) in IP-related standards work, must have been in operation for at least 3 years, must show significant deployment of its standards on the Internet, and must not require licensing fees for implementation of its significant protocols.

Additionally, to be considered international, the organization must have voting members primarily located in at least three different geographic regions and at least two different countries within each region. The proposal notes that rejected applicants can appeal to the ICANN Board, where a two-thirds majority can override the rejection.
sections.eli5: To join, a standards group has to be open to anyone, international, not-for-profit, have lots of active members, have been around for years, and have standards that are actually used and can be implemented for free.

sections.title: How the PSO Operates
sections.content:
The proposal emphasizes open proceedings and public transparency. All communications between ICANN and the PSO are made public. PSO business discussions happen on publicly-archived mailing lists. Meeting schedules are posted 90 days in advance, agendas 30 days in advance, and minutes within 30 days of meetings.

Policy development follows the Internet tradition: each SDO maintains responsibility for policies in its own protocols. The PSO serves as a forum for coordination and conflict resolution but does not impose policies unilaterally. Any policy adopted must have consensus from all SDOs.
sections.eli5: Everything is public: the discussions, the meetings, the decisions. Each standards group keeps control of its own protocols and works together to solve disagreements.

sections.title: Relationship to ICANN Governance
sections.content:
The proposal clarifies that PSO-nominated ICANN Board Directors function as full Directors of ICANN, not as representatives of the PSO. Geographically, no more than 2 PSO-nominated Directors may come from the same region. The PSO's advisory role is limited to matters that ICANN refers to it related to protocol parameter assignment.

The proposal includes a mechanism for the PSO and ICANN to periodically review the MOU and propose updates to it. The cover letter from Scott Bradner notes that the proposal benefited from extensive discussion within the IETF's IESG and IAB, as well as representatives from the ITU and W3C, positioning it as a consensus-based approach among major international Internet organizations.
sections.eli5: The people the PSO nominates to ICANN's board have to act as full board members, not just representing the PSO. And the agreement can be updated if needed, as long as everyone agrees.
